stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin end first three-way summit with a nuclear-risk pledge and no Ukraine deal
stories.summary: The presidents of the United States, China and Russia met together for the first time on Thursday in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Outlets report the meeting produced a pledge on reducing nuclear risks but no treaty and no agreement on the war in Ukraine. President Trump was due to take questions from reporters on Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: The three countries hold most of the world's nuclear weapons and are central to the wars and trade disputes that affect prices and security everywhere. The meeting set no binding limits, so those risks are largely where they were before it.
stories.background: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin had never before sat down as a group of three. China hosted this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, and the White House said in the week before that the three would hold a joint meeting there. Trump had proposed that such a meeting focus on nuclear weapons. It took place while Russia's war in Ukraine continues, with Russian strikes hitting Kyiv during and after the summit. Trump and Putin had last met in Alaska in August 2025.

facts.text: The three leaders met for about 90 minutes on Thursday in Shenzhen, according to France 24.
The Associated Press described the talks as focused on nuclear risks and said they ended without major breakthroughs.

Fox News reported the summit produced a nuclear risk pledge but no breakthrough on Ukraine; The New York Times said it produced no treaties on war or nuclear weapons and that artificial intelligence was not on the agenda.
Trump was scheduled to face reporters on Friday, Fox News reported.
Putin said on Thursday that Russia would not negotiate a limited ceasefire with Ukraine now, citing Ukrainian strikes on the bridge to Crimea.
Trump and Putin shook hands in Shenzhen on Wednesday, their first meeting since the Alaska summit in August 2025, Arab News reported.
Before the summit, the White House said the three leaders planned a joint meeting, which the AP called unprecedented.

stories.headline: Russian missiles damage Kyiv bridges after Ukraine's strikes on the Crimea bridge; missiles fall in Poland
stories.summary: Russia fired missiles and drones at Kyiv overnight into Friday, damaging bridges over the Dnipro River, cutting power and killing several people. The attack followed three Ukrainian strikes in four days on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, after which Vladimir Putin promised retaliation. Poland said Russian missiles and a drone came down on its territory during the attack.
stories.why_it_matters: The exchange hit transport links that civilians rely on in a capital city, and weapons landed inside a NATO member. Putin also said he would not negotiate a limited ceasefire now, which lowers the chances of an early pause in the fighting.
stories.background: Russia and Ukraine are at war, and Russia holds the Crimean peninsula, which it annexed from Ukraine. The Kerch Bridge links Russia to Crimea, carries rail traffic that Reuters says matters to Russian logistics, and is described by outlets as a symbol of Putin's rule there. This week's Ukrainian strikes halted rail traffic on the bridge. At the same time, U.S. envoys, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders met in Berlin to discuss terms for ending the war, and Putin met the U.S. and Chinese presidents in Shenzhen.

facts.text: A third Ukrainian strike in four days halted rail traffic on the Kerch Bridge, the AP reported.
Putin said Russia's response would be "far more painful" than the damage to the bridge and that Russia would not negotiate a limited ceasefire now.
Russian ballistic missiles damaged three bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv overnight, according to Bloomberg and the BBC.
The AP reported that the attacks on Kyiv killed three people, injured nine and cut power.
A daytime Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged St. Volodymyr's Cathedral and the Dutch and Austrian embassies.
Poland's defense minister said two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in eastern Poland on Friday, Bloomberg reported; France 24 reported Polish officials said no one was hurt.
Troops from 11 European countries are holding an exercise in southeastern Poland to prepare for a possible mission in Ukraine after the war, the AP reported.
Russia has said it will quickly restore the Kerch Bridge; engineering specialists told The New York Times the work could take years.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said new talks on Ukraine that include European leaders could be held soon on neutral ground, and Putin said Russia had invited European representatives to Moscow.

The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. envoys have discussed NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for territory in the Donbas; Russia's Sergei Ryabkov said Russia rejects any deal letting Ukraine join NATO, Bloomberg reported.

stories.headline: Myanmar rejects UN court's genocide ruling as Rohingya refugees ask when they can go home
stories.summary: A day after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, Myanmar called the decision unfair. Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh welcomed the ruling and said they want to return home, and rights groups called for sanctions. Malaysia said it plans to resettle 10,000 Rohingya in Turkey.
stories.why_it_matters: More than a million people remain in refugee camps with no date for return, and the court has no force of its own to change that. Only left-leaning and center outlets in the digest covered the ruling; no right-leaning outlet did.
stories.background: The Rohingya are a Muslim minority from Myanmar. A military campaign in 2017 drove hundreds of thousands of them out of the country, most into neighboring Bangladesh. Gambia brought a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court, under the 1948 Genocide Convention; the court ordered protective measures in 2020 and allowed the case to proceed in 2022. Myanmar has denied genocide and has described its actions as counter-terrorism. The court ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19.

facts.text: The International Court of Justice ruled on Nov. 19 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017.
Reuters, as carried by The Hindu, reported it was the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide.
Myanmar dismissed the ruling as "unfair".
Rohingya in Bangladesh welcomed the verdict and said they want to return to Myanmar, the AP reported.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya are displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in camps in Bangladesh, according to The Japan Times.
Rights groups urged sanctions on Myanmar after the ruling, the AP reported.
Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on Friday that Malaysia is seeking to resettle 10,000 Rohingya in Turkey.
In South Africa, a rights group called for a criminal investigation into the country's arms sales to Myanmar between 2017 and 2021, the Daily Maverick reported.
Human Rights Watch said before the ruling that the judgment is final and cannot be appealed.

stories.headline: Houthi attack damages Riyadh's tallest tower, home of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund
stories.summary: Saudi Arabia said a Houthi attack on Thursday damaged several floors of the tallest building in Riyadh, which houses the Public Investment Fund, and that no one was hurt. Outlets report the Houthis have stepped up attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks. Oil prices rose after the attack, Reuters reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on Saudi Arabia can push up fuel prices far from the region: oil rose on supply concerns after this one.
stories.background: The Houthis are an armed movement in Yemen backed by Iran, and outlets describe Saudi Arabia as at war with them. A United Nations-brokered truce had largely reduced hostilities since 2022 before it collapsed. Attacks on Saudi territory have resumed this year, including one on Nov. 8 that damaged an Aramco building in Riyadh's financial district. The Public Investment Fund is the state fund that manages much of Saudi Arabia's wealth and investments abroad.

facts.text: Saudi Arabia confirmed that a Houthi attack damaged Riyadh's tallest building and reported no casualties.
Saudi civil defense said the attack caused material damage to several floors of a tower in Riyadh's financial center, NBC News reported.
The 80-story building houses the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund.
Fox News, citing reports, said windows were destroyed across up to eight floors.
The Houthis have increased attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, hitting airports, energy infrastructure, military sites and Riyadh's financial district, according to The Hindu.
Oil prices rose as the attacks raised concerns about supply, Reuters reported.
On Nov. 8, an attack claimed by the Houthis damaged an Aramco tower in the same financial district, Al-Monitor reported.

stories.headline: New draft deal at UN climate talks removes all mention of fossil fuels on the final day
stories.summary: A new draft agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, no longer mentions fossil fuels. Australia, which is leading the negotiations, released the text on Thursday, and nearly 200 countries were due to finish on Friday. Campaign groups objected, and outlets differ on how close a deal is.
stories.why_it_matters: These agreements shape how fast governments move away from coal, oil and gas, which affects energy bills, jobs and the pace of warming. Only center outlets and wire services in the digest covered the draft.
stories.background: COP is the annual United Nations climate conference where nearly 200 countries negotiate joint commitments. This year's meeting, COP31, is hosted by Turkey in Antalya, with Australia running the negotiations. The future of coal, oil and gas has been the most contested question. An earlier draft released on Nov. 16 called for faster action to phase out fossil fuels, and oil-producing countries have long resisted such wording.

facts.text: The draft that Australia released on Thursday drops any mention of fossil fuels.
The draft also removes dates for reaching net zero and an earlier demand to phase out unilateral trade measures such as the European Union's carbon border tax by 2027, The Hindu reported.
Campaign groups reacted with anger to the new text, France 24 reported.
Nearly 200 countries had until Friday to reach a deal.
The Financial Times reported that the talks have turned toward carbon capture and that critics say the final sessions focus on energy security.
The earlier draft, published Nov. 16, called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels", according to Daily Sabah.

stories.headline: UK and EU meet in Brussels to agree food trade, carbon and youth mobility deals
stories.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Union leaders Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa in Brussels on Friday for a summit meant to rebuild ties after Brexit. The two sides were expected to announce deals on food trade, carbon emissions and a scheme letting young people live and work across each other's borders.
stories.why_it_matters: The deals would cut checks on food crossing between Britain and the EU and let some people aged 18 to 32 work on the other side, which affects prices, businesses and travel. No right-leaning outlet in the digest covered the summit.
stories.background: Britain voted to leave the European Union a decade ago, and its departure added checks on trade and limits on living and working across the border. A first UK-EU summit in 2025 began a process both sides call a reset. Andy Burnham, now prime minister, has said he hopes to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime and argues closer ties will help the economy. The EU side is led by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

facts.text: Burnham met von der Leyen and Costa in Brussels on Friday.
The two sides were set to agree deals on food trade, energy or carbon emissions, and youth mobility.
The youth scheme is expected to cover 100,000 people aged 18 to 32, The Hindu reported.
Burnham has said he hopes to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, France 24 reported.
The British government has said the package could add about £10 billion a year to the economy by 2040, ITV News reported in October.

stories.headline: Somalia orders the UAE ambassador to leave within 72 hours
stories.summary: Somalia's cabinet ordered the United Arab Emirates ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and recalled its own ambassador from Abu Dhabi. Reuters reported that Somalia cited an "invasion". The breakaway region of Somaliland said on Thursday that Somalia has no authority over its foreign relations.
stories.why_it_matters: A break in relations between the two governments affects port, defence and security arrangements in the Horn of Africa. No right-leaning outlet in the digest covered it.
stories.background: Somalia's federal government in Mogadishu claims authority over Somaliland, a region that conducts its own diplomatic and economic dealings and rejects that claim. Relations between Mogadishu and the United Arab Emirates were already strained before this week, according to Addis Standard. In April 2024 Somalia gave Ethiopia's ambassador 72 hours to leave in an earlier dispute over an agreement between Ethiopia and Somaliland.

facts.text: Somalia's Council of Ministers ordered the UAE ambassador to leave within 72 hours and recalled Somalia's ambassador to the UAE for consultations, Addis Standard reported.
The AP and Reuters also reported the expulsion order; Reuters said Somalia cited an "invasion".
Somaliland said on Thursday that its diplomatic, economic and strategic arrangements need no approval from Somalia, Horn Diplomat reported.

stories.headline: El Salvador's Bukele seeks a third term while his troops fight gangs in Haiti
stories.summary: El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele is seeking a third term, which Reuters called unprecedented. The move comes as Salvadoran troops operate against gangs in Haiti, where crowds have rallied to thank him and where rights monitors have raised concerns.
stories.why_it_matters: Bukele's approach to gangs is being tried in a second country, and its results will affect safety in Haiti and migration across the region. His bid for another term also tests limits on presidential power in El Salvador.
stories.background: Nayib Bukele is the president of El Salvador and has said his government finished off the gangs there. El Salvador changed its constitution to remove presidential term limits, and its legislature moved the next election from 2029 to 2027, according to the AP. Haiti has been overrun by armed gangs since 2021, the year its president, Jovenel Moise, was assassinated. Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing in a gang attack in October.

facts.text: Bukele is seeking a third term as president, Reuters and the AP reported.
Bukele said his troops attacked the home of a gang leader in Haiti, NBC News reported.
Thousands of people marched in Haiti to thank Bukele, Fox News reported; NBC News also reported celebrations.
Groups that monitor human rights have raised concerns about the operation, NBC News reported.
El Salvador removed presidential term limits from its constitution and moved its next election from 2029 to 2027, the AP reported earlier this month.
Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing in a gang attack in mid-October, the AP reported.
